chapter_title: Let Me Not to the Marriage of True Minds

concepts.title: True Minds and the Impediments Love Admits Not
concepts.definition: Shakespeare's sonnet 116 opens with the poet refusing to obstruct the marriage of true minds: love that alters when it finds alteration, or removes when the beloved departs, is not love. The phrase 'marriage of true minds' shifts marriage from bodies and contracts to faithful union of souls.
concepts.key_idea: Real love admits no impediment -- it neither bends to change nor leaves in absence.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww112.txt opening lines (marriage of true minds, admit impediments, love that alters is not love, removal bears it out)
question_patterns: what does shakespeare mean by the marriage of true minds
in class 11 let me not to the marriage of true minds: what kind of love does the poet reject
explain the phrase admit impediments in the sonnet
according to the poem when is love not really love
why does the poet talk of minds rather than bodies
what does removal mean in the context of the poem

solution_steps.explain: The poet will not stand between true minds uniting -- such love needs no permission and brooks no barrier.
Whatever alters when circumstances alter, or departs when the beloved leaves, was never love.
True love is fixed, constant -- a marriage of minds that outfaces change and distance alike.

concepts.title: The North Star and Time's Bent Sickle
concepts.definition: Love is an ever-fixed mark looked on from tempests and never shaken; it is the star to every wandering bark, whose worth is unknown though its height be taken. Time, though its bending sickle reaps lips and cheeks, cannot touch love within his brief hours and weeks -- it outlasts the doom of physical beauty.
concepts.key_idea: Love is the fixed star that weathers every tempest -- Time may harvest beauty, never constancy.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww112.txt metaphor lines (ever fixed mark, star to every wandering bark, time's bending sickle, physical beauty reaped, love alters not with time)
question_patterns: why is love compared to a star in the sonnet
in class 11 let me not to the marriage of true minds: explain the figure of time's bending sickle
what is meant by an ever fixed mark that looks on tempests
how does time fail against true love in the poem
what does the wandering bark metaphor suggest
explain love's worth although his height be taken

solution_steps.explain: Love is a beacon every storm can see but no storm can move -- permanence made visible.
Like the pole star it guides every wandering bark; its value beyond measure is known only to the faithful.
Time's sickle cuts down rosy lips and cheeks, the body's beauty, yet passes love by unchanged.

concepts.title: The Daring Couplet: If This Be Error
concepts.definition: The sonnet ends in defiance: if this be error and the poet proved mistaken, then he never wrote, and no man ever loved. The hyperbole stakes the poet's entire life and craft on love's constancy -- a wager that turns definition into declaration.
concepts.key_idea: All or nothing for love -- the poet bets his pen and mankind's heart on his definition.
concepts.textbook_ref: keww112.txt closing couplet (if this be error and upon me proved, i never writ, nor no man ever loved)
question_patterns: explain the final couplet of the sonnet
in class 11 let me not to the marriage of true minds: what does the poet stake in the last two lines
is the ending a proof or a challenge discuss
why does shakespeare claim no man ever loved if his definition fails
what is the effect of the hyperbole in the closing couplet
how does the couplet summarise the whole sonnet's argument

solution_steps.explain: The poet says: if my account of love is error, then wipe out my writings and every love ever felt.
The exaggeration is rhetorical -- it claims such constancy is the common experience of lovers.
The couplet turns a cool definition into a ringing personal declaration -- form serving argument.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Explain the double metaphor of love as an ever-fixed mark and as the star to every wandering bark.

solution_template.explain: An ever-fixed mark is a beacon or landmark: visible through tempests, unmoved by them.
The guiding star steers every wandering ship; sailors measure its height though its worth is beyond measure.
Together the images give love both stability -- it does not move -- and guidance -- it orients the lost.

worked_examples.question_pattern: Time is personified as a reaper in the sonnet. Explain the personification and its effect.

solution_template.explain: Time carries a bending sickle like Father Time, harvesting what grows -- rosy lips and cheeks.
The sickle's reach is physical beauty, which fades within time's brief hours and weeks.
Love escapes the harvest: it does not alter with time's hours and weeks, but endures to the edge of doom.
